label: lem:radial-monotonicity
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Radial monotonicity

title: Proof
body_md:
The monotonicity of $G$ follows from \eqref{eq:g-positive} and the constant
extension.  We include the quotient arguments, following the calculation
in \cite{MengWang2024}.

In noncompact type, set
\[
  s(r)=g'(r)-\coth r\,g(r).
\]
The regular expansion of the degree-one solution at the pole gives
$s(0+)=0$, while $s(R)=-\coth R\,g(R)<0$.  If $s$ were positive somewhere,
 it would have a positive interior maximum at a point $r_0$.  At that point
$s'(r_0)=0$, and combining this identity with \eqref{eq:radial-ode} gives
\begin{align*}
 0={}&\bigl(m\coth r_0+(k-1)\tanh r_0\bigr)g'(r_0)\\
 &+\left(\lambda_R-m\operatorname{csch}^2r_0+(k-1)\operatorname{sech}^2r_0\right)g(r_0).
\end{align*}
Since $s(r_0)>0$, we have $g'(r_0)>\coth r_0g(r_0)$.  Substitution in the
 preceding equality would imply
\[
 m\operatorname{csch}^2r_0-(k-1)\operatorname{sech}^2r_0-\lambda_R
 >m\coth^2r_0+(k-1),
\]
which is impossible.  Hence $s\le0$ and $g/\sinh r$ is nonincreasing on
$(0,R)$.  The constant extension preserves the conclusion for $r\ge R$.

In compact type, put
\[
  s(r)=g'(r)-(\cot r-\tan r)g(r).
\]
Again $s(0+)=0$ and $s(R)<0$.  At a hypothetical positive interior maximum
$r_0\in(0,R)$, the equations $s'(r_0)=0$ and
\eqref{eq:radial-ode} yield
\begin{align*}
 0={}&(m\cot r_0-k\tan r_0)g'(r_0)\\
 &+\left(\lambda_R-\frac{m-k}{\sin^2r_0}
 -\frac{k}{\sin^2r_0\cos^2r_0}\right)g(r_0).
\end{align*}
On $(0,\pi/4)$ the first coefficient is positive, and $s(r_0)>0$ implies
$g'(r_0)>(\cot r_0-\tan r_0)g(r_0)$.  A direct simplification then gives
\[
  \lambda_R<2(m+k).
\]
This contradicts the ball estimate $\lambda_R\ge2(m+k)$ for
$R\le\pi/4$ proved in \cite{AithalSanthanam1996}; see also
\cite[Lemma 4.1]{MengWang2024}.  Hence $g/(\sin r\cos r)$ is
nonincreasing.  It is strictly decreasing after $R$ because $G$ is constant
there.

Finally, in noncompact type
\[
 \frac{G^2}{\sinh^2r},\qquad
 \frac{G^2}{\sinh^2r\cosh^2r}
\]
are nonincreasing.  In compact type the second angular weight equals
$(G/(\sin r\cos r))^2$, and the first equals this function times
$\cos^2r$; both are nonincreasing on $(0,\pi/4)$.

label: thm:hopf-projection
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:hopf-projection}
There is a linear map
\[
  \Pi:\operatorname{Sym}(V)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Sym}(V)
\]
with the following properties.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.2em]
 \item $\Pi$ is positive, unital, trace-preserving, Hilbert--Schmidt
 self-adjoint, and idempotent.
 \item For every $\xi\in S(V)$,
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:Q-via-Pi}
   Q_\xi=k\Pi(P_\xi)-P_\xi.
 \end{equation}
 \item The complex-linear extension of $\Pi$ to $M_m(\mathbb C)$ is a positive
 unital map.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently, if
\begin{equation}\label{eq:C-def}
  \mathcal C:=k\Pi-I,
\end{equation}
then $\mathcal C$ is positive on real positive semidefinite matrices,
$\mathcal C(P_\xi)=Q_\xi$, $\mathcal C(I)=(k-1)I$, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:C-spectral-splitting}
 \mathcal C=(k-1)I\quad\text{on }\operatorname{Ran}\Pi,
 \qquad
 \mathcal C=-I\quad\text{on }\operatorname{Ker}\Pi.
\end{equation}
head: environment
name: Canonical Hopf projection

label: eq:Pi-associative
title: Proof
body_md:
We first treat $\mathbb K=\mathbb R,\mathbb C,\mathbb H$.  Regard $V$ as $\mathbb K^n$ with its standard
real inner product.  Let $J_0=I$ and let $J_1,\ldots,J_{k-1}$ be right
multiplication by an orthonormal basis of the imaginary part of $\mathbb K$.  Thus
all $J_\alpha$ are orthogonal, and the imaginary ones are skew-symmetric.
Define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Pi-associative}
  \Pi(A)=\frac1k\sum_{\alpha=0}^{k-1}
  J_\alpha A J_\alpha^{\mathsf T}.
\end{equation}
For $\mathbb K=\mathbb C$ or $\mathbb H$, the conjugations
$A\mapsto J_\alpha A J_\alpha^{\mathsf T}$ form a finite group after signs
are discarded.  Hence their average is the orthogonal projection onto the
common fixed-point space.  This proves idempotence and Hilbert--Schmidt
self-adjointness.  Positivity, unitality, and trace preservation follow
immediately from \eqref{eq:Pi-associative}.  The same formula on complex
matrices is an average of unitary conjugations and is therefore positive and
unital.

For a unit vector $\xi$, the vectors
$J_0\xi,\ldots,J_{k-1}\xi$ form an orthonormal basis of the real $k$-plane
$\mathbb K\xi$.  Therefore
\[
  \Pi(P_\xi)=\frac1k\sum_{\alpha=0}^{k-1}P_{J_\alpha\xi}
  =\frac1kP_{\mathbb K\xi}.
\]
Since the Hopf space is $\mathcal V_\xi=\mathbb K\xi\ominus\mathbb R\xi$, we have
$Q_\xi=P_{\mathbb K\xi}-P_\xi$, proving \eqref{eq:Q-via-Pi}.

We next treat the Cayley plane.  Use the real spin representation
$V=\mathbb R^{16}$ of $\operatorname{Spin}(9)$.  Choose a symmetric Clifford system
$S_0,\ldots,S_8$ satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{eq:clifford-system}
  S_\alpha S_\beta+S_\beta S_\alpha
  =2\delta_{\alpha\beta}I.
\end{equation}
The matrices $I,S_0,\ldots,S_8$ are mutually orthogonal for the
Hilbert--Schmidt product, each with squared norm $16$.  Define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Pi-cayley}
  \Pi(A)=\frac1{16}\left((\operatorname{tr} A)I+
  \sum_{\alpha=0}^{8}\operatorname{tr}(AS_\alpha)S_\alpha\right).
\end{equation}
Thus $\Pi$ is the Hilbert--Schmidt projection onto
$\operatorname{span}\{I,S_0,\ldots,S_8\}$; in particular it is self-adjoint and
idempotent.  It is unital and trace-preserving because
$\operatorname{tr} S_\alpha=0$.

For $\xi\in S^{15}$, put
$a_\alpha=\left\langle S_\alpha\xi,\xi\right\rangle$ and
$S(a)=\sum_{\alpha=0}^8a_\alpha S_\alpha$.  The standard Clifford-system
model of the octonionic Hopf fibration gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:octonionic-hopf-identity}
  \sum_{\alpha=0}^{8}a_\alpha^2=1,
  \qquad S(a)\xi=\xi;
\end{equation}
see \cite{FerusKarcherMunzner1981,OrneaPartonPiccinniVuletescu2013}.
By \eqref{eq:clifford-system}, $S(a)^2=I$.  Its $+1$ eigenspace has real
dimension $8$ and is the octonionic line through $\xi$.  Denoting its
orthogonal projection by $P_{\mathbb O\xi}$, we obtain
\[
  P_{\mathbb O\xi}=\frac12(I+S(a)),
  \qquad
  \Pi(P_\xi)=\frac1{16}(I+S(a))=\frac18P_{\mathbb O\xi}.
\]
It follows that $8\Pi(P_\xi)-P_\xi=Q_\xi$, which is
\eqref{eq:Q-via-Pi} for $k=8$.

The last formula also proves positivity of $\Pi$ on real symmetric
matrices, because every positive semidefinite matrix is a nonnegative
linear combination of real rank-one projections.  To verify the positivity
needed for operator Jensen's inequality, extend \eqref{eq:Pi-cayley}
complex-linearly.  For a complex unit vector $z$, the numbers
$a_\alpha=z^*S_\alpha z$ are real.  Since
$S(a)^2=|a|^2I$ and
\[
  |a|^2=z^*S(a)z\le \left\lVert S(a)\right\rVert=|a|,
\]
we have $|a|\le1$.  Hence
\[
  \Pi(zz^*)=\frac1{16}(I+S(a))\succeq0.
\]
By spectral decomposition, the complex extension is positive on all
Hermitian positive semidefinite matrices.

Finally, \eqref{eq:C-spectral-splitting} follows from $\Pi^2=\Pi$.  Since
$\mathcal C(P_\xi)=Q_\xi\succeq0$, the real rank-one decomposition also shows
that $\mathcal C$ is positive on every real positive semidefinite matrix.
head: environment

label: cor:hopf-algebra
title: Corollary
head: environment
name: Algebraic consequences

title: Proof
body_md:
The trace identity follows from trace preservation of $\Pi$.  Write
$X=X_1+X_0$ with $X_1=\Pi X\in\operatorname{Ran}\Pi$ and
$X_0=(I-\Pi)X\in\operatorname{Ker}\Pi$.  The decomposition is Hilbert--Schmidt
orthogonal, and \eqref{eq:C-spectral-splitting} gives
\[
 \operatorname{tr}(X\mathcal C(X))=(k-1)\left\lVert X_1\right\rVert_{\mathrm{HS}}^2
 -\left\lVert X_0\right\rVert_{\mathrm{HS}}^2
 \le(k-1)\left\lVert X\right\rVert_{\mathrm{HS}}^2.
\]
The first isotropy identity is standard.  Apply \eqref{eq:Q-via-Pi}, use
linearity, and use $\Pi(I)=I$ to obtain the second.

label: lem:trace-ritz
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Trace Ritz principle

title: Proof
body_md:
The matrix $M$ is the $L^2$ Gram matrix, hence is positive definite.  If
$a^{\mathsf T}Ka=0$, then the function
$P_a=\sum_i a_iP_i$ has zero weak gradient and is constant on the connected
domain $\Omega$.  Its mean is zero, so it vanishes.  Linear independence
then gives $a=0$, and $K$ is positive definite.

Let $0<\eta_1\le\cdots\le\eta_m$ be the Ritz values of the Neumann
quadratic form restricted to $\operatorname{span}\{P_1,\ldots,P_m\}$.  Since this trial
space is contained in the orthogonal complement of the constants, the
min--max principle gives $\mu_j(\Omega)\le\eta_j$.  The $\eta_j$ are the
generalized eigenvalues of $Ka=\eta Ma$, so their reciprocals are the
eigenvalues of $K^{-1/2}MK^{-1/2}$.  Therefore
\[
  \sum_{j=1}^{m}\frac1{\mu_j(\Omega)}
  \ge\sum_{j=1}^{m}\frac1{\eta_j}
  =\operatorname{tr}(K^{-1/2}MK^{-1/2})=\operatorname{tr}(K^{-1}M).
\]
head: environment

label: lem:weinberger-center
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Weighted Weinberger center

title: Proof
body_md:
Set
\[
  \Phi(t)=\int_0^tG(s)\,\mathrm d s.
\]
In noncompact type consider
$\mathscr F(p)=\int_\Omega\Phi(\operatorname{dist}(p,x))\,\mathrm dv(x)$.  Since $G$ is bounded
and eventually equal to the positive constant $g(R)$, $\Phi(t)$ has linear
growth with positive slope.  The boundedness of $\Omega$ therefore implies
$\mathscr F(p)\to\infty$ as $p$ escapes to infinity.  Thus $\mathscr F$
has a minimizer $o$.  The first variation of distance and dominated
convergence give, for every $v\in T_oM$,
\[
  D\mathscr F(o)[v]
  =-\int_\Omega G(r_o(x))\left\langle v,\xi_o(x)\right\rangle\,\mathrm dv(x).
\]
The derivative vanishes at a minimizer, proving \eqref{eq:center-vector}.
This energy-minimization form of the centering argument is analogous to
\cite{Laugesen2021}.

In compact type let
$C=\overline{B_{i(M)/4}(q)}$.  This ball lies strictly inside the convexity
radius and is strongly geodesically convex.  The same functional is
well-defined on $C$, because the distance between two points of $C$ is at
most $\pi/4$, and it attains a minimum there.  If a minimizer $p$ lay on
$\partial C$, every minimizing geodesic from $p$ to a point of the open set
$\Omega\subset C$ would initially point into $C$.  If $\nu$ denotes the
outer normal of $\partial C$, this gives
$\left\langle \xi_p(x),\nu\right\rangle<0$ on a set of positive measure.  Hence
\[
 D\mathscr F(p)[-\nu]
 =\int_\Omega G(r_p(x))\left\langle \xi_p(x),\nu\right\rangle\,\mathrm dv(x)<0,
\]
contradicting minimality.  The minimizer is therefore interior and its
first variation vanishes in every direction.  This proves
\eqref{eq:center-vector}.  The distance estimate follows from the triangle
inequality and $i(M)=\pi/2$.
head: environment

label: lem:trial-admissible
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:trial-admissible}
The functions $P_1,\ldots,P_m$ belong to $H^1(\Omega)$, have zero mean, and
are linearly independent in $L^2(\Omega)$.  Their mass and stiffness
matrices in \eqref{eq:mass-stiffness-def} are therefore positive definite,
and \eqref{eq:trace-ritz} applies.
head: environment
name: Admissibility of the coupled trial family

title: Proof
body_md:
Equation \eqref{eq:center-vector} gives the zero-mean conditions.  At the
pole, regularity of the degree-one solution gives
$G(r)=g'(0)r+O(r^3)$.  Hence $G(r)/r$ and $G'(r)$ are locally bounded, and
\eqref{eq:angular-bilinear} shows that $P_v$ has locally square-integrable
gradient.  Away from the pole the assertion is immediate, while outside
$B_R(o)$ the radial derivative vanishes.  Thus $P_v\in H^1(\Omega)$.

Suppose $P_v=0$ almost everywhere.  The function has a continuous
representative, so it vanishes on $\Omega$.  For $r>0$, $G(r)>0$; hence
$\left\langle v,\xi\right\rangle=0$ for every point of a nonempty open subset in polar
coordinates.  If $v\ne0$, the corresponding equatorial set of directions
has empty interior, a contradiction.  Therefore $v=0$, proving linear
independence.  The last statement follows from \cref{lem:trace-ritz}.
head: environment

label: lem:ray-rearrangement
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:ray-rearrangement}
Let $I=(0,L)$, where $L\le\infty$, and let $J>0$ be locally integrable.
Set
\[
  V(t)=\int_0^tJ(s)\,\mathrm d s,
\]
and let $\tau$ be the inverse of $V$ on its range.  If $E\subset I$ is
measurable, put $Y(E)=\int_EJ(r)\,\mathrm d r$.  For a continuous weight $w$ for
which the following integrals are finite, define
\[
  F(y)=\int_0^{\tau(y)}w(r)J(r)\,\mathrm d r.
\]
Then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.2em]
 \item if $w$ is nondecreasing,
 \[
  \int_EwJ\,\mathrm d r\ge F(Y(E)),
 \]
 and $F$ is convex;
 \item if $w$ is nonincreasing,
 \[
  \int_EwJ\,\mathrm d r\le F(Y(E)),
 \]
 and $F$ is concave.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently, for $Y_R=V(R)$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tangent-increasing}
 F(y)\ge F(Y_R)+w(R)(y-Y_R)
\end{equation}
when $w$ is nondecreasing, while the inequality is reversed when $w$ is
nonincreasing.  If $w$ is strictly decreasing and equality holds in the
rearrangement for $0<Y(E)<V(L)$, then
$E=(0,\tau(Y(E)))$ modulo $J(r)\,\mathrm d r$-null sets.
head: environment
name: Weighted ray rearrangement and tangent line

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $I_y=(0,\tau(y))$.  Since $E$ and $I_{Y(E)}$ have the same
$J(r)\,\mathrm d r$ measure, the exchanged parts
$E\setminus I_{Y(E)}$ and $I_{Y(E)}\setminus E$ have the same measure.  An
increasing weight is no smaller on the first set than on the second, while
a decreasing weight is no larger.  This proves the two rearrangement
inequalities.  Strict monotonicity gives the equality statement by the same
exchange argument.

Since $F'(y)=w(\tau(y))$, the derivative is nondecreasing or nonincreasing
with $y$.  This proves convexity or concavity and the corresponding tangent
inequalities.
head: environment

label: prop:stiffness-comparison
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Coupled stiffness comparison

label: eq:q-ray-upper
title: Proof
body_md:
For a ray $E_\xi$, set
\[
 q(\xi)=\int_{E_\xi}G'(r)^2J(r)\,\mathrm d r.
\]
Since $G'=0$ for $r>R$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:q-ray-upper}
  q(\xi)\le Q_R.
\end{equation}

Consider first noncompact type.  By
\cref{lem:radial-monotonicity}, both weights
\[
  \frac{G^2}{\sinh^2r}
  \quad\text{and}\quad
  \frac{G^2}{\sinh^2r\cosh^2r}
\]
are nonincreasing.  The rearrangement and concave tangent inequalities give
\begin{align}
 \int_{E_\xi}\frac{G^2}{\sinh^2r}J\,\mathrm d r
 &\le H_{0,R}^-+d(Y(\xi)-Y_R),
 \label{eq:h0-ray-noncompact}\\
 \int_{E_\xi}\frac{G^2}{\sinh^2r\cosh^2r}J\,\mathrm d r
 &\le H_{1,R}^-+f(Y(\xi)-Y_R),
 \label{eq:h1-ray-noncompact}
\end{align}
where
\[
 f=\frac{c}{\sinh^2R\cosh^2R}=d-e.
\]
Substitute \eqref{eq:q-ray-upper}--\eqref{eq:h1-ray-noncompact} into
\eqref{eq:K-exact}.  The constant part is
\begin{align*}
 &Q_R\int P_\xi\,\mathrm d\sigma
 +H_{0,R}^-\int(I-P_\xi-Q_\xi)\,\mathrm d\sigma
 +H_{1,R}^-\int Q_\xi\,\mathrm d\sigma\\
 &\hspace{20mm}=\frac{|\mathbb S^{m-1}|}{m}
 \left(Q_R+(m-k)H_{0,R}^-+(k-1)H_{1,R}^-\right)I\\
 &\hspace{20mm}=\lambda_RaI
\end{align*}
by \eqref{eq:ball-energy-identity}.  The imbalance part is
\begin{align*}
 &d\int(Y-Y_R)(I-P_\xi-Q_\xi)\,\mathrm d\sigma
 +f\int(Y-Y_R)Q_\xi\,\mathrm d\sigma\\
 &\qquad=-dZ-dW+fW=-dZ-eW,
\end{align*}
where \eqref{eq:volume-balance-rays} was used.  This proves
\eqref{eq:K-upper-noncompact}.

In compact type the same argument uses the decreasing weights
\[
  \frac{G^2}{\sin^2r}
  \quad\text{and}\quad
  \frac{G^2}{\sin^2r\cos^2r}.
\]
Their endpoint values are $d$ and
\[
 f=\frac{c}{\sin^2R\cos^2R}=d+e.
\]
The constant part is again $\lambda_RaI$, whereas the imbalance part is
\[
  -dZ-dW+fW=-dZ+eW.
\]
This proves \eqref{eq:K-upper-compact}.
head: environment

label: lem:stiffness-rigidity
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Rigidity of the stiffness comparison

title: Proof
body_md:
The proof of \cref{prop:stiffness-comparison} writes $T_\pm-K$ as the
integral of three nonnegative scalar deficits multiplying the mutually
orthogonal positive semidefinite projections
$P_\xi$, $I-P_\xi-Q_\xi$, and $Q_\xi$.  In particular, the radial part is
\[
  (Q_R-q(\xi))P_\xi,
  \qquad Q_R-q(\xi)\ge0.
\]
If the integral matrix is zero, its trace is zero.  The trace integrand is
nonnegative, so $q(\xi)=Q_R$ for almost every $\xi$.  Since
$G'(r)=g'(r)>0$ on $(0,R)$, this implies
$(0,R)\subset E_\xi$ modulo null sets.  Hence $Y(\xi)\ge Y_R$ almost
everywhere.  The volume balance \eqref{eq:volume-balance-rays} forces
$Y(\xi)=Y_R$, and no radial measure can remain outside $(0,R)$.  This proves
\eqref{eq:ray-ball-ae} and then the polar-coordinate identity gives
$|\Omega\triangle B_R(o)|=0$.

For completeness, suppose first that a point of the open set $\Omega$ lies
outside the open ball $B_R(o)$.  A sufficiently small neighborhood has
positive measure outside the ball, contradicting the null symmetric
difference; the same argument applies to a point of $\Omega$ on
$\partial B_R(o)$.  Hence $\Omega\subset B_R(o)$.  Conversely, a point of
$B_R(o)\setminus\Omega$ either has a neighborhood disjoint from $\Omega$,
or lies on the smooth hypersurface $\partial\Omega$.  In both cases the
complement of $\Omega$ has positive measure in a small ball, again a
contradiction.  Thus $B_R(o)\subset\Omega$.
head: environment

label: lem:aligned-closure
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Aligned trace-free closure

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $T=\lambda aI-dZ$.  From $0<K\preceq T$ and $M\succeq0$,
\[
  \operatorname{tr}(K^{-1}M)\ge\operatorname{tr}(T^{-1}M)
  \ge\operatorname{tr}\bigl(T^{-1}(aI+cZ)\bigr).
\]
Diagonalize $Z$, with eigenvalues $z_1,\ldots,z_m$.  The last trace is
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{i=1}^{m}\frac{a+cz_i}{\lambda a-dz_i}
 &=\frac m\lambda+
 \frac{d+\lambda c}{\lambda}
 \sum_{i=1}^{m}\frac{z_i}{\lambda a-dz_i}.
\end{align*}
The function $z\mapsto z/(\lambda a-dz)$ is strictly convex on the
positivity interval, and $\sum_i z_i=0$.  Jensen's inequality proves
\eqref{eq:aligned-conclusion}.

If equality holds, strict convexity gives $z_i=0$ for every $i$, so
$Z=0$ and $T=\lambda aI$.  Equality in the second trace comparison and
$T^{-1}>0$ imply $M=aI$.  Since $M$ is then positive definite, equality
in the first comparison implies $K^{-1}=T^{-1}$ and hence
$K=\lambda aI$.
head: environment

label: lem:positive-projection-jensen
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Positive-projection Jensen inequality

label: eq:H-nonnegative
title: Proof
body_md:
Set
\[
  Y=uX+v\Pi X,
  \qquad T=I-Y.
\]
Since $\Pi^2=\Pi$,
\[
  \Pi Y=(u+v)\Pi X,
  \qquad
  X=\frac1uY-\frac{v}{u(u+v)}\Pi Y.
\]
Define
\[
 H=\operatorname{tr}\bigl((I-Y)^{-1}Y\bigr),
 \qquad
 D=\operatorname{tr}\bigl((I-Y)^{-1}\Pi Y\bigr).
\]
Trace preservation and $\operatorname{tr} X=0$ give $\operatorname{tr} Y=0$.  If
$y_1,\ldots,y_m<1$ are the eigenvalues of $Y$, then strict convexity of
$t\mapsto t/(1-t)$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:H-nonnegative}
  H=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\frac{y_i}{1-y_i}\ge0,
  \qquad H=0\Longleftrightarrow Y=0.
\end{equation}

We claim that $D\le H$.  On the open convex set $I-A\succ0$, let
\[
  \Phi(A)=-\log\det(I-A).
\]
Convexity and the derivative
$D\Phi(Y)[B]=\operatorname{tr}((I-Y)^{-1}B)$ give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Phi-gradient}
 \operatorname{tr}\bigl((I-Y)^{-1}(Y-\Pi Y)\bigr)
 \ge \Phi(Y)-\Phi(\Pi Y).
\end{equation}
Since $\Pi$ is positive and unital,
$I-\Pi Y=\Pi(I-Y)\succ0$.  The function $t\mapsto-\log t$ is
operator convex.  The Davis--Choi--Jensen inequality
\cite{HansenPedersen2003} therefore yields
\[
 -\log(I-\Pi Y)
 \preceq\Pi\bigl(-\log(I-Y)\bigr).
\]
Taking traces and using trace preservation gives
$\Phi(\Pi Y)\le\Phi(Y)$.  The left-hand side of
\eqref{eq:Phi-gradient} is $H-D$, proving the claim.

Finally,
\begin{align*}
 \operatorname{tr}\bigl(T^{-1}(I+X)\bigr)-m
 &=\operatorname{tr}\bigl((I-Y)^{-1}(X+Y)\bigr)\\
 &=\left(1+\frac1u\right)H-
   \frac{v}{u(u+v)}D\\
 &\ge\left(1+\frac1{u+v}\right)H\ge0.
\end{align*}
This proves \eqref{eq:positive-projection-jensen}.  Equality forces $H=0$
and hence $Y=0$.  The linear operator $uI+v\Pi$ acts by $u+v$ on
$\operatorname{Ran}\Pi$ and by $u$ on $\operatorname{Ker}\Pi$, so it is invertible; consequently
$X=0$.  The converse is immediate.
head: environment

label: lem:positive-mass-closure
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Positive-mass closure

title: Proof
body_md:
Set
\[
 N=T^{-1/2}\widehat M T^{-1/2},
 \qquad B=T^{-1/2}AT^{-1/2}.
\]
Then $N\succeq0$ and $N\succeq B$.  Because $0<T\preceq2I$, the matrix
$P=2T-T^2$ satisfies $0\preceq P\preceqI$.  Therefore
\[
 \operatorname{tr} N\ge\operatorname{tr}(PN)\ge\operatorname{tr}(PB).
\]
The second inequality follows from $P\succeq0$ and $N-B\succeq0$.  Since
$P$ commutes with $T$, cyclicity of the trace gives
\[
 \operatorname{tr}(PB)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl((2I-T)A\bigr)
 =2\operatorname{tr} A-\operatorname{tr}(TA)\ge2m-m=m.
\]
Since $\operatorname{tr} N=\operatorname{tr}(T^{-1}\widehat M)$, the proof is complete.

label: prop:compact-endpoints
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:compact-endpoints}
Under \cref{ass:compact-localization}, the estimate
\eqref{eq:main-compact} holds when $k=1$ or $n=1$, and equality
characterizes geodesic balls.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $k=1$, then $Q_\xi=0$ and $\mathcal C=0$, so
\eqref{eq:K-upper-compact} reduces to
\[
  K\preceq\lambda_RaI-dZ.
\]
Together with \eqref{eq:M-lower}, the hypotheses of
\cref{lem:aligned-closure} are satisfied.

If $n=1$, then $Q_\xi=I-P_\xi$.  Equations
\eqref{eq:volume-balance-rays} and \eqref{eq:n-one-W-minus-Z} give
$W=-Z$, and hence
\[
  K\preceq\lambda_RaI-(d+e)Z.
\]
Again \cref{lem:aligned-closure} applies.  In either case,
\cref{lem:trace-ritz} gives \eqref{eq:main-compact}.  If equality holds,
the equality part of the matrix lemma yields equality in the stiffness
comparison; \cref{lem:stiffness-rigidity} then gives
$\Omega=B_R(o)$.  The converse is immediate.
head: environment

label: eq:compact-radius-assumption-proof
title: Proof
body_md:
By \cref{prop:compact-endpoints}, only the case $1<k<m$ remains.  Assume
\begin{equation}\label{eq:compact-radius-assumption-proof}
  \cot^2R\ge k-1.
\end{equation}
Normalize the mass matrix and the stiffness comparator by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:compact-normalization}
 \widehat M=\frac1aM,
 \qquad X=\frac caZ,
 \qquad
 \alpha=\frac{d}{\lambda_Rc}=\frac1{\lambda_R\sin^2R},
 \qquad
 \beta=\frac{e}{\lambda_Rc}=\frac1{\lambda_R\cos^2R}.
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Mhat-lower}
  \widehat M\succeq0,
  \qquad \widehat M\succeqI+X,
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:compact-T-def}
  0<K\preceq\lambda_RaT,
  \qquad
  T=I-\alpha X+\beta\mathcal C(X)\succ0.
\end{equation}
The radius condition is equivalent to
\begin{equation}\label{eq:alpha-ge-kminus1-beta}
  \alpha\ge(k-1)\beta.
\end{equation}

We verify the remaining hypotheses of
\cref{lem:positive-mass-closure}.  From \eqref{eq:X-order-bound} and
positivity of $\mathcal C$,
\[
  -\alpha X\preceq\alpha\rhoI,
  \qquad
  \beta\mathcal C(X)\preceq
  \beta(m-1)(k-1)\rhoI.
\]
Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{eq:T-upper-before-two}
 T\preceq
 \left[1+\rho\bigl(\alpha+(m-1)(k-1)\beta\bigr)\right]I.
\end{equation}
The compact angular weights are nonincreasing, so their integrals over
$(0,R)$ are bounded below by their endpoint values times $Y_R$.  The ball
identity \eqref{eq:ball-energy-identity} consequently gives
\begin{align*}
 \lambda_RA_R
 &\ge Y_R\bigl((m-k)d+(k-1)(d+e)\bigr)\\
 &=Y_R\bigl((m-1)d+(k-1)e\bigr).
\end{align*}
After division by $\lambda_RA_R$, this becomes
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rho-bound-compact}
  \rho\bigl((m-1)\alpha+(k-1)\beta\bigr)\le1.
\end{equation}
Moreover, \eqref{eq:alpha-ge-kminus1-beta} implies
\[
 \alpha+(m-1)(k-1)\beta
 \le(m-1)\alpha+(k-1)\beta.
\]
Combining this with \eqref{eq:T-upper-before-two} and
\eqref{eq:rho-bound-compact} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:T-upper-two}
  0<T\preceq2I.
\end{equation}

Next, \eqref{eq:Z-trace-free}, \eqref{eq:C-trace}, and
\eqref{eq:C-quadratic-bound} imply
\begin{align}
 \operatorname{tr}\bigl(T(I+X)\bigr)
 &=m-\alpha\operatorname{tr}(X^2)+\beta\operatorname{tr}\bigl(X\mathcal C(X)\bigr)\notag\\
 &\le m-\bigl(\alpha-(k-1)\beta\bigr)\operatorname{tr}(X^2)\notag\\
 &\le m.
 \label{eq:TA-compact}
\end{align}
Thus \cref{lem:positive-mass-closure}, applied to
\eqref{eq:Mhat-lower}, \eqref{eq:T-upper-two}, and
\eqref{eq:TA-compact}, yields
\[
  \operatorname{tr}(T^{-1}\widehat M)\ge m.
\]
By \eqref{eq:compact-T-def} and the inverse Loewner order,
\[
 \operatorname{tr}(K^{-1}M)
 \ge\frac1{\lambda_R}\operatorname{tr}(T^{-1}\widehat M)
 \ge\frac m{\lambda_R}.
\]
The trace Ritz principle proves \eqref{eq:main-compact}.

If equality holds in the spectral inequality, all terms in the chain
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^{m}\frac1{\mu_j(\Omega)}
 \ge\operatorname{tr}(K^{-1}M)
 \ge\frac1{\lambda_R}\operatorname{tr}(T^{-1}\widehat M)
 \ge\frac m{\lambda_R}
\]
are equal.  Since $M\succ0$, equality in the inverse-order comparison
forces $K=\lambda_RaT$, namely equality in the compact stiffness
comparison.  By \cref{lem:stiffness-rigidity}, $\Omega=B_R(o)$.  The
converse is immediate.

  \cot^2(\pi/8)=3+2\sqrt2>3,

body_md:
If $\Pi Z=0$, then $\mathcal C(Z)=-Z$.  The compact stiffness estimate becomes
\[
  K\preceq\lambda_RaI-(d+e)Z.
\]
Together with \eqref{eq:M-lower}, this is exactly the setting of

label: prop:abstract-obstruction
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:abstract-obstruction}
Assume $1<k<m$ and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:bad-radius}
  \cot^2R<k-1.
\end{equation}
Let
\begin{equation}\label{eq:obstruction-alpha-beta}
  \alpha=\frac1{\lambda_R\sin^2R},
  \qquad
  \beta=\frac1{\lambda_R\cos^2R}.
\end{equation}
Then there exists a nonzero trace-free $X\in\operatorname{Ran}\Pi$ such that
$I+X\succ0$ and
\[
  T=I-\alpha X+\beta\mathcal C(X)\succ0,
\]
but
\begin{equation}\label{eq:obstruction-trace}
  \operatorname{tr}\bigl(T^{-1}(I+X)\bigr)<m.
\end{equation}
Consequently, the abstract implications
\[
  \widehat M\succeq0,
  \quad \widehat M\succeqI+X,
  \quad 0<K\preceq T
  \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
  \operatorname{tr}(K^{-1}\widehat M)\ge m
\]
are false in the range \eqref{eq:bad-radius}.
head: environment
name: Finite-dimensional obstruction

label: eq:T-I-plus-sX
title: Proof
body_md:
There is a nonzero trace-free element of $\operatorname{Ran}\Pi$: in the complex and
quaternionic cases with $n\ge2$, one may take a real symmetric
$\mathbb K$-linear operator with $\mathbb K$-diagonal entries $1,-1,0,\ldots,0$; in the
Cayley case one may take any $S_\alpha$ from
\eqref{eq:clifford-system}.  For $X\in\operatorname{Ran}\Pi$,
$\mathcal C(X)=(k-1)X$, so
\begin{equation}\label{eq:T-I-plus-sX}
  T=I+sX,
  \qquad s=(k-1)\beta-\alpha>0.
\end{equation}
The ball lower bound $\lambda_R\ge2(m+k)$ and $R\le\pi/4$ imply
\[
  0<s<\frac{2(k-1)}{\lambda_R}<1.
\]
After multiplying a fixed nonzero trace-free element of $\operatorname{Ran}\Pi$ by a
sufficiently small scalar, both $I+X$ and $I+sX$ are positive definite.

Let $x_1,\ldots,x_m$ be the eigenvalues of $X$.  Then
$\sum_i x_i=0$ and
\[
 \operatorname{tr}\bigl(T^{-1}(I+X)\bigr)
 =\sum_{i=1}^{m}h_s(x_i),
 \qquad h_s(t)=\frac{1+t}{1+st}.
\]
Because $0<s<1$,
\[
  h_s''(t)=-\frac{2s(1-s)}{(1+st)^3}<0
\]
on the relevant interval.  Strict concavity and $X\ne0$ give
\[
  \frac1m\sum_{i=1}^{m}h_s(x_i)
  <h_s\left(\frac1m\sum_i x_i\right)=h_s(0)=1,
\]
which is \eqref{eq:obstruction-trace}.  Taking
$\widehat M=I+X$ and $K=T$ proves the final assertion.

label: lem:imbalance-realization
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Realization of small imbalance directions

title: Proof
body_md:
Define the desired ray volume by
\[
  Y_\varepsilon(\xi)=Y_R+\varepsilon\left\langle A\xi,\xi\right\rangle.
\]
For small $|\varepsilon|$ this is positive and lies in the range of $V$.  Since
\[
  \int_{S(V)}\left\langle A\xi,\xi\right\rangle\,\mathrm d\sigma
  =\frac{|\mathbb S^{m-1}|}{m}\operatorname{tr} A=0,
\]
the total volume is unchanged.  Put
$r_\varepsilon(\xi)=V^{-1}(Y_\varepsilon(\xi))$ and take the radial graph
$0<r<r_\varepsilon(\xi)$.  It is smooth for small $\varepsilon$ and centrally symmetric
because $Y_\varepsilon(-\xi)=Y_\varepsilon(\xi)$; in particular $o$ is a Weinberger
center.

The fourth-moment identity on the sphere is
\[
 \int_{S^{m-1}}\xi_i\xi_j\xi_p\xi_q\,\mathrm d\sigma
 =\frac{|\mathbb S^{m-1}|}{m(m+2)}
 (\delta_{ij}\delta_{pq}+\delta_{ip}\delta_{jq}
 +\delta_{iq}\delta_{jp}).
\]
Using $\operatorname{tr} A=0$ in the definition of $Z$ gives
\eqref{eq:Z-realization}.  The localization statement follows by uniform
convergence $r_\varepsilon\to R$.
head: environment

label: rem:cayley-obstruction
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:cayley-obstruction}
Let $M=\mathbb{O}\mathrm P^2$ and
\[
  R_*<R<\frac\pi8,
  \qquad R_*=\arctan\frac1{\sqrt7}.
\]
Take $X=tS_0$, where $S_0$ is one member of the Clifford system and
$0<t<1$.  Then $X\in\operatorname{Ran}\Pi$, $\operatorname{tr} X=0$, and the eigenvalues of $X$ are
$t$ and $-t$, each with multiplicity eight.  Since $\mathcal C(X)=7X$, put
$s=7\beta-\alpha\in(0,1)$.  Formula \eqref{eq:T-I-plus-sX} gives
\[
 \operatorname{tr}\bigl(T^{-1}(I+X)\bigr)
 =8\frac{1+t}{1+st}+8\frac{1-t}{1-st}<16.
\]
By \cref{lem:imbalance-realization}, the same matrix direction occurs for
arbitrarily small smooth star-shaped perturbations that remain inside the
original localization range.  This does not disprove the full spectral
inequality: the exact mass and stiffness matrices retain nonlinear raywise
remainders that are absent from the affine model.
